chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: Left behind by the bus, catching up by Trailways, and Jordan's $150 advance
summary: He and the band's one white trombonist miss the departure, reach the dance late, and Jordan gives him money anyway.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Anyway, I got all those things together as quick as I could, and I got this taxi and made it up there with... As a matter of fact, I must have had about, oh, twenty dollars or

something like that. Anyway, I got this taxi and went up to the hotel where they were leaving. And I get there... I kept looking at my watch. And I made it, I guess, about 20 minutes after 9. Well, knowing bands, I said, "Well, maybe they're still around" or something. But I didn't know Louis Jordan. When Louis Jordan said "time," it meant on time. When I got there, the desk clerk told me, "Oh, Mr. Jordan, the band, they left about a half-hour ago." So then my heart fell.

While I'm sitting up there talking, this fellow came downstairs. He was a White fellow, a trombone player. He was the only White musician in the band. He and I had talked the night that I played before. I saw him, and I was kind of glad, you know. He saw me and laughed. "Hey, man, you got left, too!" I said, "Yeah, man. As a matter of fact, I didn't know until a couple of hours ago that I was going anywhere." He said, "Yeah. Well, that's Louis." I said, "Well, what are you going to do?" He said, "I'm going down to the Greyhound Bus Station -- I know where they are. And we'll make it."

So we went down to the Greyhound Bus station, and find out that they have no buses going to this place. We had to go to the Trailways Bus station. And they had a bus, luckily enough, that was leaving in a couple of hours.
Anyway, we get this bus, and we go down, and we get there

to the dance where they're playing, just about ten minutes after they hit the first number. And we both went in expecting to catch hell from Louis or something like that -- I didn't know him. But we went in and put on our uniforms, and got up on the bandstand, and played.

After we finished that night, I was ready with my apology to him, explaining why I didn't make it on time for the bus. And I never got it out. Because I went into the dressing room after we finished the dance, and he made some comment that I sounded good that night, and he went in his pocket and I think he gave me something like one hundred fifty dollars. He said, 'Here's some money until you get your first paycheck.' So it kind of gave me a different view of the very tough Louis Jordan.

But he was the kind of guy that wanted things the way he wanted it, and he didn't mind paying for it. And if he didn't seem very sympathetic at times about what your excuses were for something, although you knew he understood what you were talking about... He would come up with some statement like, 'Well, that's your problem, and you got a problem and I have a business.'
Anyway, I felt differently about him when he gave me this money and everything, and I felt more at home. I sent some back here to look after my kid. And we went out on the tour,
